subject: geography
topicDisplay: Geographic Themes Freshwater Oceans Coastal Margins Extreme Environments Geophysical Hazards Leisure Tourism Sport Food Health Urban Environments
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Peatlands are significant carbon stores because:
options: Waterlogged anaerobic conditions slow decomposition, accumulating organic carbon
They release carbon faster than they store it when undisturbed
questions.explain: Saturated, oxygen-poor peat slows microbial decay, allowing organic carbon to build up over millennia.

questions.q: What is an 'energy pathway'?
options: The route by which energy travels from producer to consumer
The career of an energy engineer
A walking route to a power station
questions.explain: An energy pathway is the flow of an energy resource, such as a gas pipeline or oil tanker route, from source to market.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes a 'near place' from a 'far place'?
options: Near places feel geographically and emotionally close, while far places feel distant or alien
Near places are richer; far places are poorer
Near places are always rural; far places are always urban
Near places exist; far places are imaginary
questions.explain: Near and far refer to perceived closeness, both in physical distance and in emotional or cultural familiarity, not just kilometres.

questions.q: Which statement about the link between the water and carbon cycles is correct?
options: They operate entirely independently of each other
Vegetation links them by both transpiring water and fixing carbon
The carbon cycle has no influence on climate
Water has no role in carbon transfer
questions.explain: Plants couple the cycles: photosynthesis fixes carbon while transpiration moves water, and both respond to climate.

questions.q: Which force, generated by the sinking of a dense, cold oceanic plate at a subduction zone, is now regarded as the dominant driver of plate motion?
questions.explain: Slab pull arises as a cold, dense subducting slab sinks into the mantle and is considered the most significant force moving plates.

questions.q: In the Park (hazard-response) model, the curve plots quality of life or economic activity against:
options: Time, through pre-disaster, disruption, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction phases
questions.explain: Park's model shows quality of life over time across stages from relief through rehabilitation to reconstruction.

questions.q: Solifluction, common in periglacial areas, is:
options: The plucking of bedrock by glaciers
The slow downslope flow of saturated soil over frozen ground
The rapid sliding of dry rock down a cliff
questions.explain: Solifluction is the slow movement of waterlogged active-layer soil over impermeable permafrost on slopes.

questions.q: How does climate change threaten water security?
options: It has no effect on water
It alters precipitation patterns, shrinks glaciers and increases droughts and floods
questions.explain: Warming shifts rainfall, melts the glaciers that feed rivers, and intensifies both droughts and floods, stressing water supplies.

questions.q: Which margin type is associated with the deepest-focus earthquakes and explosive andesitic volcanoes?
questions.explain: Subduction at an oceanic-continental destructive margin produces a Benioff zone of deep earthquakes and explosive andesitic stratovolcanoes.

questions.q: Why can large dam projects create both benefits and conflicts?
options: They provide power and water storage but can displace people and reduce downstream flow
questions.explain: Dams deliver hydropower and storage yet can flood communities, alter ecosystems and reduce water reaching downstream users.

questions.q: A formal representation of a place is best illustrated by:
options: A novel set in the town
Census data and Ordnance Survey maps
questions.explain: Formal representations are objective and often statistical, such as census data, official maps and government reports.

questions.q: What is the 'circular economy'?
options: A system that designs out waste by reusing, recycling and remanufacturing resources
Trade that only flows in one direction
An economy based only on circular coins
questions.explain: The circular economy keeps materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling, contrasting with the linear take-make-dispose model.

questions.q: In the disaster-risk (risk = hazard x vulnerability / capacity) equation, risk is reduced by:
questions.explain: Because capacity to cope is the denominator, raising it lowers overall disaster risk.

questions.q: Which is a key challenge in feeding a growing global population?
options: Balancing rising demand with limited land, water and the impacts of climate change
questions.explain: Producing enough food for a growing population while constrained by finite land and water and a changing climate is a central challenge.

questions.q: An 'experienced place' differs from a 'media place' because an experienced place is:
options: One a person has visited or lived in first-hand
One only ever seen on television or film
questions.explain: Experienced places are those a person has direct, lived contact with, whereas media places are known only second-hand through representation.

questions.q: How might the success of a regeneration scheme be measured economically?
options: By the number of road signs replaced
Through changes in employment rates and average household income
By counting the number of pigeons
questions.explain: Economic success indicators include changes in employment, income levels, business start-ups and inward investment.

questions.q: Which of the following is a demographic measure of regeneration success?
options: The price of bus tickets only
Changes in the age structure and population numbers of an area
questions.explain: Demographic indicators include changes in population size, age structure and the reduction of out-migration.

questions.q: Eustatic sea-level change is best defined as:
options: A change in the level of the land relative to the sea
A global change in the volume of water in the oceans
questions.explain: Eustatic change is a worldwide change in sea level caused by changes in ocean water volume, e.g. from ice melt.

questions.q: Resilience to tectonic hazards is best described as the ability of a community to:
options: Absorb, adapt to and recover from a hazard event
Predict the exact time of every earthquake
questions.explain: Resilience is the capacity to withstand, adapt to and bounce back from a hazard impact.

questions.q: What is meant by 'resource security'?
options: Owning all of a country's mines
A reliable, affordable and sustainable supply of a needed resource
questions.explain: Resource security is the assured access to enough of a resource at an affordable price to meet a population's needs.

questions.q: The moment magnitude scale (Mw) is logarithmic; an increase of one whole unit represents roughly how much more energy released?
questions.explain: Each whole step on the magnitude scale corresponds to about a 32-fold increase in energy released.

questions.q: An 'insider' perspective on a place is characterised by:
options: Viewing the place only through media representations
Knowing only the formal statistical data about it
Treating the place purely as a tourist destination
A sense of belonging, familiarity and identity with the place
questions.explain: An insider feels they belong to a place and experiences it as familiar, holding an identity bound up with it.

questions.q: Which of the following would most likely be an 'outsider's' representation of a place?
options: A national newspaper article written by a visiting journalist
questions.explain: Outsider representations come from those without a deep personal attachment, such as journalists, tourists or distant media.

questions.q: Government deprivation-led regeneration policy typically targets places with:
options: High scores on the Index of Multiple Deprivation
The lowest levels of multiple deprivation
questions.explain: Regeneration is often directed at areas scoring highly for multiple deprivation, indicating concentrated social and economic problems.

questions.q: Which seismic wave type is the fastest and is the first to be recorded at a seismograph?
questions.explain: P-waves are compressional and travel fastest, so they arrive first at a seismometer.

questions.q: Ridge push (gravitational sliding) operates because newly formed oceanic lithosphere at a mid-ocean ridge is:
options: Denser and colder than older lithosphere
Elevated and slides down the sloping asthenosphere away from the ridge
questions.explain: At ridges the hot, raised lithosphere slides down the flanks under gravity, pushing the plate away from the ridge axis.

questions.q: A criticism of flagship, property-led regeneration is that it can:
options: Create benefits that fail to 'trickle down' to deprived local residents
Always benefit the original community equally
questions.explain: Such schemes are criticised because new wealth often does not trickle down to existing low-income communities.

questions.q: Within the carbon cycle, which is correctly described as a slow (long-term) carbon store?
options: Soil organic matter turning over annually
questions.explain: Carbon locked in sedimentary rock is part of the slow carbon cycle, residing there for millions of years.

questions.q: Why does increased atmospheric CO2 represent a disruption to the natural carbon budget?
options: The oceans instantly absorb all additional CO2
Vegetation growth removes it within one season
Anthropogenic emissions exceed the rate at which natural sinks can absorb them
It is fully offset by silicate weathering within months
questions.explain: Human emissions outpace the uptake capacity of land and ocean sinks, so atmospheric CO2 accumulates.

questions.q: Which process represents biological carbon sequestration on land?
options: Photosynthesis fixing CO2 into plant tissue
questions.explain: Photosynthesis removes atmospheric CO2 and stores the carbon as biomass, a key terrestrial sequestration pathway.
